description.content:
Registration, login, session lookup and email verification.

### Email verification rule (important)

The register controller only sends a verification email when the request body contains `role: "customer"` **explicitly**.

| Body `role` | `isEmailVerified` | Verification email | Can log in immediately? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"customer"` | `false` | Sent | No — verify first |
| `"admin"` | `true` | Not sent | Yes |
| omitted | `true` (role still defaults to `customer`) | Not sent | Yes |

So for quick local testing, omit `role` and you get a usable customer account with no SMTP round-trip.

Creates a **customer** account and emails a verification link.

`Public` — no token required.

### Body

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | ✅ | Trimmed |
| `email` | string | ✅ | Unique, lowercased, must match `x@y.z` |
| `password` | string | ✅ | Min 6 chars, hashed with bcrypt before saving |
| `role` | `customer` \| `admin` | ❌ | Defaults to `customer` |
| `phone` | string | ❌ | **Unique** across users — reuse causes a duplicate-key error |
| `address` | object | ❌ | `street`, `city`, `state`, `zip`, `country` |

### Responses

**201 Created**
```json
{
  "message": "User registered successfully. Please verify your email to activate your account.",
  "user": {
    "id": "66f0...",
    "name": "Ali Haider",
    "email": "customer@example.com",
    "role": "customer",
    "isEmailVerified": false
  }
}
```

**400 Bad Request** — `{ "message": "Name, email and password are required" }` or `{ "message": "User already exists" }`

### Notes

- Because `role` is `customer` here, login stays blocked with `403` until the email is verified.
- If SMTP vars (`EMAIL_HOST`, `EMAIL_USER`, `EMAIL_PASS`) are missing, the account is still created but no mail goes out — a warning is logged. Grab the token straight from the `emailVerificationToken` field in MongoDB in that case.

### Responses

**201 Created**
```json
{
```

`isEmailVerified` is omitted from the response for non-customer roles, but is stored as `true`.

Exchanges email + password for a session **cookie**.

`🌍 Public` — no token required.

> **This is the request that powers the whole collection.** The JWT is no longer in the response body — it comes back as an httpOnly cookie which Postman stores in its cookie jar and replays automatically.

### Body

| Field | Type | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `email` | string | ✅ |
| `password` | string | ✅ |

### Responses

**200 OK**
```json
{
  "message": "Login successfully",
  "data": {
    "id": "66f0...",
    "name": "Admin User",
    "email": "admin@example.com",
    "role": "admin",
    "isEmailVerified": true
  }
}
```

| Status | Body | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | `Email and password are required` | Missing field |
| `401` | `Invalid email or password` | Wrong credentials (same message for unknown email — deliberate) |
| `403` | `Please verify your email before logging in` | `isEmailVerified` is `false` |

### The cookie

```
Set-Cookie: token=<jwt>; Max-Age=604800; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
```

- **httpOnly** — page JavaScript cannot read it, so an XSS bug cannot steal the session.
- **Max-Age 604800** — 7 days, the same as the JWT expiry.
- `secure` + `SameSite=None` when `NODE_ENV=production`; `SameSite=Lax` in development.

Nothing sets a failed login's cookie — a `401` / `403` response carries no `Set-Cookie` at all.

### Clients

| Client | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Postman | Nothing — the cookie jar handles it (**Cookies** link under Send) |
| Browser (fetch) | `fetch(url, { credentials: "include" })` |
| Browser (axios) | `axios.defaults.withCredentials = true` |
| Mobile / server-to-server | Read the `Set-Cookie` value, or keep using `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` — the header path still works |

CORS must name your exact frontend origin (`http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:5173` are allowed by default) — `origin: '*'` cannot be combined with credentials.

description.content:
Clears the session cookie.

`🌍 Public` — deliberately **not** behind `authenticate`.

Why no auth: if the JWT has already expired, the user still needs the cookie removed from their browser. Requiring a valid token would leave a dead cookie sitting there. Logging out twice is therefore harmless — it always answers `200`.

### Response — 200 OK
```json
{ "message": "Logout successfully" }
```

```
Set-Cookie: token=; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
```

> **JWT is stateless.** This removes the cookie from the client; it does not revoke the token server-side. Anyone who copied the raw JWT beforehand can keep using it until it expires. Real revocation needs a token blacklist or short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens.

description.content:
Returns the full user document for whoever owns the current session.

`🔒 Authenticated` — any role. The token is read from the `token` cookie first, then from an `Authorization: Bearer` header.

### Responses

**200 OK**
```json
{
  "_id": "66f0...",
  "name": "Admin User",
  "email": "admin@example.com",
  "role": "admin",
  "address": { "city": "Karachi", "country": "Pakistan" },
  "phone": "03009999999",
  "isEmailVerified": true,
  "createdAt": "2026-08-06T10:15:00.000Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-08-06T10:15:00.000Z"
}
```

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `401` | `Authentication required` (neither cookie nor `Bearer` header), `Invalid token`, or `Token expired` |
| `404` | Token is valid but the user was deleted |

Flips `isEmailVerified` to `true` and clears the stored token.

`Public` — no auth header; the query-string token *is* the credential.

### Query params

| Param | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `token` | ✅ | Signed JWT sent in the verification email. Valid for **24 hours**. |

### How to get the token locally

The email links to `FRONTEND_URL/verify-email?token=...`. Two ways to grab it without a frontend:

1. Open the email and copy the `token` query param out of the link.
2. No SMTP configured? Read it straight from Mongo:
   ```js
   db.users.findOne({ email: "customer@example.com" }, { emailVerificationToken: 1 })
   ```

Paste it into the `verification_token` environment variable and send.

### Responses

| Status | Body |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | `{ "message": "Email verified successfully" }` |
| `400` | `Verification token is required` / `Invalid or expired verification token` / `Verification token has expired` |

The endpoint is single-use: the token is nulled after success, so a second call returns `400`.
The JWT from the verification email link (24 h expiry).

Emails a one-hour password reset link.

`🌍 Public`

### Body
| Field | Type | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `email` | string | ✅ |

### Response — 200 OK (always the same)
```json
{ "message": "If an account exists for that email, a password reset link has been sent." }
```

The answer never changes, whether the email exists or not — otherwise this route becomes a tool for discovering which emails are registered (user enumeration).

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `Email is required` |

The link points at `${FRONTEND_URL}/reset-password?token=<jwt>` (`FRONTEND_URL` defaults to `http://localhost:5173`). With no SMTP configured, the backend logs the link to its console instead of sending it — that is how you test this locally.

Sets a new password using the token from the reset email.

`🌍 Public`

### Body
| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `token` | string (JWT) | ✅ | From the email link's `?token=` |
| `password` | string | ✅ | At least 6 characters |

### Response — 200 OK
```json
{ "message": "Password reset successfully. Please log in with your new password." }
```

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `Token and new password are required` |
| `400` | `Password must be at least 6 characters` |
| `400` | `Password reset link has expired` (older than 1 hour) |
| `400` | `Invalid password reset link` (bad signature) |
| `400` | `Invalid or already used password reset link` |

**One-time use.** The token is also stored on the user document and cleared on success, so the same link cannot be replayed even while its JWT is still valid. The current session cookie is cleared too, forcing a fresh login.

`slug` is generated automatically from `name` (lowercased, spaces → hyphens) whenever the document is saved through `.create()` or `.save()`.

Returns categories in one of **two modes**. The response tells you which one you got via `mode`.

`🌍 Public`

### 1. `tree` — the default

Every category, nested through `parentCategory`, each parent carrying a `subCategories` array. This is what a navigation menu needs, so it is never paginated: half a tree loses the parent–child links.

```json
{
  "message": "Categories fetched successfully.",
  "mode": "tree",
  "data": [
    {
      "_id": "66f1...",
      "name": "Electronics",
      "slug": "electronics",
      "image": "/uploads/66f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1.png",
      "parentCategory": null,
      "subCategories": [
        { "_id": "66f2...", "name": "Laptops", "slug": "laptops", "parentCategory": "66f1...", "subCategories": [] }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

### 2. `flat` — the shared query engine

Search, filter, sort, paginate and field-limit, with `parentCategory` populated to `{ name, slug }`. Meant for an admin table.

Switch on with `?flat=true`, or simply by sending `search`, `page` or `limit` — those three are meaningless in tree mode, so they flip it automatically.

```json
{
  "message": "Categories fetched successfully.",
  "mode": "flat",
  "data": [
    { "_id": "66f2...", "name": "Laptops", "parentCategory": { "_id": "66f1...", "name": "Electronics", "slug": "electronics" } }
  ],
  "pagination": { "total": 15, "page": 1, "limit": 10, "totalPages": 2, "hasNextPage": true, "hasPrevPage": false }
}
```

| Query | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `?flat=true` | Flat list, no other params needed |
| `?search=lap` | Regex over `name` and `description` (implies flat) |
| `?parentCategory=66f1...` | Direct children of one category |
| `?parentCategory=null` | Root categories only |
| `?sort=name&limit=50` | Alphabetical page of 50 |

The test script stores the first item's `_id` in `{{category_id}}`, which the product requests reuse — it works in either mode.

item.name: Get All Products (search, filter, sort, paginate)

description.content:
Lists active products with full query support.

`🌍 Public`

### Query parameters

| Param | Example | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `page` | `2` | Page number (min `1`, default `1`) |
| `limit` | `20` | Page size (default `10`, **max `100`**) |
| `sort` | `-price`, `category,-price` | Multi-field sort; `-` = descending. Default `-createdAt` |
| `fields` | `name,price` / `-description,-images` | Include or exclude fields |
| `search` | `laptop` | Case-insensitive regex over `name` and `description` |
| `<field>` | `category=66f1...` | Exact-match filter on any schema field |
| `<field>[gte\|gt\|lte\|lt\|ne]` | `price[gte]=100` | Range / comparison filter |
| `<field>[in]` | `status[in]=a,b` | `$in` — comma-separated |
| `<field>[nin]` | `status[nin]=a,b` | `$nin` — comma-separated |

Combine freely: `?search=phone&price[gte]=200&price[lte]=800&sort=price&page=1&limit=5`

### Response — 200 OK
```json
{
  "message": "Products fetched successfully.",
  "data": [
    {
      "_id": "66f2...",
      "name": "Gaming Laptop",
      "description": "16GB RAM, RTX 4060",
      "price": 1499.99,
      "category": { "_id": "66f1...", "name": "Electronics", "slug": "electronics" },
      "stock": 12,
      "images": ["/uploads/66f2a1....png"],
      "sku": "LAP-001",
      "isActive": true,
      "createdAt": "2026-08-06T10:25:00.000Z"
    }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "total": 42,
    "page": 1,
    "limit": 10,
    "totalPages": 5,
    "hasNextPage": true,
    "hasPrevPage": false
  }
}
```

### Security notes

- Keys starting with `$` are stripped from filters, so NoSQL operator injection through query params is blocked.
- Regex metacharacters in `search` are escaped (ReDoS protection).
- `isActive: true` is forced server-side and cannot be overridden by the client.
Page number. Min 1. Default 1.
Page size. Default 10, hard cap 100.
Comma-separated fields. Prefix with '-' for descending. Default '-createdAt'.
Case-insensitive regex across name and description.
Whitelist fields, or exclude with '-description,-images'.
Exact-match filter on any schema field.
Range filter — becomes $gte.
Range filter — becomes $lte.

| `status` | `pending`, `processing`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` | `pending` |
| `paymentMethod` | `card`, `cod`, `paypal` | `cod` |
| `paymentStatus` | `pending`, `paid`, `failed`, `refunded` | `pending` |

### Searching

`?search=` works on both sides, but matches different things:

| Caller | `search` matches |
| --- | --- |
| admin | customer **name**, customer **email**, or **order id** |
| customer | **order id** only — every order in the list is already theirs |

**Order id.** Both the full 24-character id and the short form the UI shows (`#77EA296E` — the last 8 characters) work, with or without the `#`, in either case. A full id is matched directly against `_id` (indexed). A fragment is matched with `$expr` + `$toString`, which cannot use an index — fine at this scale, but it is a collection scan, so do not point it at a very large orders collection without adding a stored short-id field.

**Customer name / email.** `name` lives on `User`, not on `Order`, and MongoDB cannot regex across collections in a plain `find`. The controller does it in two steps: find the matching users, then filter orders by `user: { $in: [...] }`.

The two are OR-ed together for admins, so one box covers both. A customer's search is still AND-ed with their own `user` filter — searching another customer's order id returns nothing, never someone else's order. If nothing matches, the result is an empty list — never the unfiltered one.

- **customer** → only orders where `user` matches the token's id

Product comments & reviews. A comment always belongs to **one product** and **one user**.

| Method | Path | Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/comments` | 🌍 public — admin token also reveals hidden comments |

| `GET` | `/api/products/:productId/comments` | 🌍 public — threads + rating summary |
| `POST` | `/api/comments` | 🔒 authenticated |
| `POST` | `/api/products/:productId/comments` | 🔒 authenticated |
| `PATCH` | `/api/comments/:id` | 🔒 owner, or admin |
| `DELETE` | `/api/comments/:id` | 🔒 owner, or admin |

### Schema

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `product` | ObjectId → `Product` | Required. Product must exist and be `isActive: true` |
| `user` | ObjectId → `User` | Always taken from the token — a client-supplied `user` is ignored |
| `text` | string | Required, 2–1000 characters |
| `rating` | number \| null | `1`–`5`. `null` = a plain comment that does not affect the average |
| `parentComment` | ObjectId → `Comment` | `null` = top-level. Set = a reply (**one level deep only**) |
| `isActive` | boolean | Default `true`. Only an admin can flip it — a hidden comment disappears from public reads and drops out of the average |

### Rules

- A user may leave **many** text-only comments on a product but only **one rating** — change it with `PATCH` instead of posting again.
- A reply can never carry a rating; one is silently dropped on create, and rejected with `400` on update.
- **Replying to a reply is allowed and lands in the same thread.** If `parentComment` points at a reply, the server re-parents the new comment to that reply's own parent, so threads are always exactly two levels deep — the Facebook model. The client shows who is being answered by prefixing the text with `@Name`; no error is returned and no deeper nesting is ever created.
- Deleting a comment also deletes its replies; deleting a product deletes all of its comments.

### Link to Product

`Product` keeps two derived fields, `averageRating` and `numReviews`, which the Comment model recalculates after every create / update / delete. Because they live on the product document you can sort and filter with them directly:

- `GET /api/products?sort=-averageRating`
- `GET /api/products?averageRating[gte]=4`

`GET /api/products/:id` also returns a `comments` array — the 10 newest visible top-level comments, populated through a virtual (comment ids are **not** stored inside the product document).

Flat, paginated list of every comment across all products. Same query engine as products (search / filter / sort / paginate / field-limit).

Persistent notifications for the logged-in user — customer **or** admin — backing the bell in both portals.

| Method | Path | Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/notifications` | 🔒 authenticated |
| `PATCH` | `/api/notifications/:id/read` | 🔒 authenticated |
| `PATCH` | `/api/notifications/read-all` | 🔒 authenticated |

### Why they are stored at all

Socket.IO only reaches clients that are connected *right now*. A customer who was offline when a product was added, or an admin who closed the portal overnight, would never learn about it — and every notification would vanish on refresh. So each notification is written to MongoDB first and emitted second: the socket is the live copy, the database is the record.

### One document, many readers

A broadcast to 10,000 customers must not write 10,000 rows:

| `user` | `audience` | Who sees it | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| an ObjectId | (ignored) | just that user | `order:status`, the customer's `order:payment` |
| `null` | `all` | every customer | `product:new` |
| `null` | `admins` | every admin | `order:new`, the admin's `order:payment` |

`audience` is only consulted when `user` is `null`, so documents written before the field existed still behave correctly.

`GET` filters by the caller's **role**: an admin gets `audience: "admins"`, everyone else gets `"all"` — plus their own targeted ones either way. So a customer never sees "New order #ABC" and an admin never sees "New product added" (they created it).

`readBy` tracks who has read each row and is never sent to the client (it holds other users' ids); the response carries a computed `read` boolean instead. One admin marking a new-order notification read does not clear it for the other admins.

`order:payment` deliberately writes **two** records — customer and admins — because the wording and the link differ (`/orders/:id` vs `/orders?order=:id`, which opens the drawer in the admin table).

Guests get live toasts but no records: notifications belong to a user.

Your notifications plus broadcasts, newest first, with an unread count so the bell badge needs only this one request.

description.content:
Card payments through **Stripe Checkout** (Stripe's hosted page).

| Method | Path | Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/payments/config` | 🌍 public |
| `POST` | `/api/payments/checkout-session` | 🔒 authenticated |
| `POST` | `/api/payments/webhook` | Stripe only (signature verified) |

### How the flow hangs together

1. Customer checks out with `paymentMethod: "card"` → the order is created normally, `paymentStatus: "pending"`.
2. Frontend calls **Create Checkout Session** and redirects the browser to the returned `url`.
3. Customer pays on Stripe's page. Card details never touch this server.
4. Stripe redirects back to `${FRONTEND_URL}/orders/:id?payment=success` (or `?payment=cancelled`).
5. Stripe calls the **webhook**, and *that* is what marks the order paid — never the success URL, which a customer could open by hand.

### Local testing

```bash
stripe login
stripe listen --forward-to localhost:5000/api/payments/webhook
# copy the printed whsec_... into STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, restart the backend
stripe trigger checkout.session.completed
```

Without `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` the whole feature stays switched off: `config` reports `cardPaymentsEnabled: false`, the other two routes answer `503`, and the storefront disables its Card option.

Tells the frontend whether card payments can be offered, and hands it the Stripe publishable key.

`🌍 Public`

```json
{ "cardPaymentsEnabled": true, "publishableKey": "pk_test_...", "currency": "pkr" }
```

`cardPaymentsEnabled` is simply "is `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` set on the server". The storefront greys out its Card option when this is `false`.

The publishable key is served from here rather than baked into the frontend's own `.env`: both keys then live in one place (`backend/.env`), and rotating them needs no frontend rebuild. It is public by design — the secret key never leaves the server.

Creates (or re-uses) a Stripe PaymentIntent for an order and returns its `clientSecret`. This is what the storefront's in-page card form uses.

`🔒 Authenticated` — the order's owner, or an admin.

### Body
| Field | Type | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orderId` | ObjectId | ✅ |

### Response — 200 OK
```json
{
  "message": "Payment intent created",
  "clientSecret": "pi_3ABC..._secret_XYZ",
  "amount": 2499900,
  "currency": "pkr"
}
```

`amount` is in the smallest unit (paisa) and is computed from the **stored order** — the client cannot influence what is charged.

**Re-used, not recreated.** If the order already has an intent that is still payable, it is retrieved (and its amount updated if needed) instead of creating a new one, so refreshing the page does not litter the Stripe dashboard with abandoned intents.

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `orderId is required`, `This order is already paid`, `This order was cancelled` |
| `403` | Someone else's order |
| `409` | The order's existing intent is already `succeeded`/`processing` — the payment is in flight and the webhook has not landed. Creating another intent here could double-charge, so it is refused |
| `404` | No such order |
| `502` | Stripe rejected the call — the real reason is in the server log |
| `503` | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is not set |

Hand `clientSecret` to `<Elements>` on the client; the order is still only marked paid by the webhook.

Asks Stripe directly whether the order's PaymentIntent succeeded, and updates the order to match.

`🔒 Authenticated` — the order's owner, or an admin.

### Why this exists

The webhook is the source of truth, but it needs `stripe listen` locally and can lag in production — leaving a customer who just paid staring at `pending`. The storefront calls this immediately after `confirmPayment()` succeeds, so the order flips to paid at once.

It is **not** a way for the client to declare a payment done: the only thing the client supplies is the order id. The server fetches the PaymentIntent from Stripe and updates the order only when

- `intent.status === "succeeded"`, **and**
- `intent.amount_received` equals the order total in the smallest currency unit

Both this route and the webhook call the same `markOrderPaid()` helper, so they can never drift apart, and both are idempotent — an order that is already paid emits no second notification.

### Responses

```json
{ "message": "Payment confirmed", "order": { "status": "processing", "paymentStatus": "paid" }, "updated": true }
```

| `message` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Payment confirmed` | Stripe said succeeded and the amount matched — order updated |
| `Payment already confirmed` | The webhook got there first; nothing to do |
| `Payment is still processing` | Stripe has not settled it yet |
| `Payment has not completed yet` | Any other intent status (returned with `paymentIntentStatus`) |

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | No payment has been started for this order |
| `403` | Someone else's order |
| `404` | No such order |
| `502` | Stripe lookup failed — real reason in the server log |
| `503` | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is not set |

Creates a Stripe Checkout session for an existing order and returns its URL.

`🔒 Authenticated` — the order's owner, or an admin.

### Body
| Field | Type | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orderId` | ObjectId | ✅ |

### Response — 200 OK
```json
{
  "message": "Checkout session created",
  "url": "https://checkout.stripe.com/c/pay/cs_test_...",
  "sessionId": "cs_test_..."
}
```

Redirect the browser to `url` (a full page navigation, not a client-side route).

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `orderId is required`, `This order is already paid`, `This order was cancelled` |
| `401` | Not logged in |
| `403` | Someone else's order |
| `404` | No such order |
| `502` | Stripe rejected the request — the real reason is in the server log, the client gets a generic message on purpose (Stripe's own errors mention the API key) |
| `503` | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is not set |

Line items are built from the **stored order**, whose prices came from the product catalogue — the client cannot influence the amount charged.

**Do not send this from Postman** — it will fail signature verification. It is documented here so the contract is visible; use the Stripe CLI to exercise it.

`Stripe only` · mounted **before** `express.json()` with `express.raw()`, and outside the rate limiter.

### Why raw body
Stripe signs the exact bytes it sent. `express.json()` would parse them into an object and `xss()` would sanitize them — either one breaks the signature. So this one route is registered ahead of both, in `server.js`.

### Events handled
| Event | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `checkout.session.completed` | `paymentStatus → paid`; a `pending` order also moves to `processing`; emits `order:payment` (customer + admins) and `order:status` (customer) |
| `checkout.session.expired` | `paymentStatus → failed` (only if still `pending`) |
| `payment_intent.payment_failed` | same as above |

The order id comes from `metadata.orderId` (falling back to `client_reference_id`), both set when the session was created.

### Responses
| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | `{ "received": true }` — including for events we ignore, and for an order that no longer exists (otherwise Stripe retries forever) |
| `400` | Signature verification failed |
| `503` | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` or `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` missing |

Replays are safe: an order already marked `paid` is left alone.

Serves a file from `backend/uploads/`.

`🌍 Public` — no auth, no rate-limit exemption.

Category and product records store a relative path like `/uploads/66f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1.png`. Prefix it with `{{base_url}}` to get a usable URL.

Set `uploaded_file_name` in the environment to the filename portion (for example `66f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1.png`).

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | Binary image response |
| `404` | File not found on disk |

Filenames are generated as a fresh Mongo ObjectId plus the original extension, so uploads never collide or leak the original filename.

description.content:
# Bano Qabil 5.0 — E-Commerce Backend API

REST API for the MERN e-commerce project (Express 5 + Mongoose + JWT).

---

## Base URL

All requests use the `{{base_url}}` environment variable.

| Environment | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Local | `http://localhost:5000` |

The port comes from `PORT` in `backend/.env` (defaults to `3000` if unset).

## Authentication

The API uses a **JWT in an httpOnly cookie**.

1. Call **Auth → Login**. The response body contains **no token** — the JWT arrives as `Set-Cookie: token=<jwt>; HttpOnly`. Postman keeps it in its cookie jar and replays it on every later request.
2. Call **Auth → Logout** to clear it.

`authenticate` reads the token from the `token` cookie first, and falls back to an `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` header — so mobile apps, server-to-server calls and the collection-level bearer auth all keep working.

Token payload: `{ id, email, role }` · Expiry: **7 days** · Signed with `JWT_SECRET`.

Why a cookie: `httpOnly` means page JavaScript cannot read the token, so an XSS bug cannot walk off with the session the way it can with `localStorage`. The trade-off is CSRF exposure — mitigated here by `SameSite=Lax` (`None` + `secure` in production) and a CORS allow-list of exact origins.

## Query engine on list routes

`GET /api/products`, `/api/orders`, `/api/comments`, `/api/users` and `/api/categories?flat=true` all run through one shared helper, so they take the same parameters:

| Param | Example | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `page` / `limit` | `?page=2&limit=20` | Pagination — default `10`, max `100` |
| `pagination` | `?pagination=false` | Return the **whole** result set, no paging. The response shape does not change: `pagination.paginated` is `false`, and `page`/`limit` describe the full set |
| `sort` | `?sort=-createdAt,name` | Multi-field sort, `-` = descending |
| `fields` | `?fields=name,price` | Include, or `?fields=-description` to exclude |
| `search` | `?search=laptop` | Case-insensitive regex over that route's search fields |
| `<field>` | `?role=admin` | Equality filter |
| `<field>[gte\|gt\|lte\|lt\|ne]` | `?price[gte]=100` | Comparison |
| `<field>[in\|nin]` | `?status[in]=pending,paid` | Comma-separated list |

Every one of them answers with the same envelope:

```json
{ "message": "...", "data": [ ... ], "pagination": { "total": 42, "page": 1, "limit": 10, "totalPages": 5, "hasNextPage": true, "hasPrevPage": false } }
```

## Roles

| Role | Capabilities |
| --- | --- |
| `customer` | Own profile, own orders, read products & categories |
| `admin` | Everything, plus user management and product/category writes |

## Standard error responses

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | Validation failure / duplicate record |
| `401` | Missing, malformed or expired token |
| `403` | Authenticated but role or ownership check failed |
| `404` | Resource not found |
| `429` | Rate limit exceeded |
| `500` | Unhandled server error |

Error body is always: `{ "message": "..." }`

## Rate limiting

**100 requests per 15 minutes per IP**, applied globally. Responses include the standard `RateLimit-*` headers. Exceeding it returns `429` with the plain-text body `Too many requests from this IP, please try again later.`

## File uploads

Image uploads use `multipart/form-data` through Multer.

- Images only (`image/*` mimetype), max **5 MB** per file
- Saved to `backend/uploads/`, stored in Mongo as a relative path such as `/uploads/68f3...c1.png`
- Served publicly at `{{base_url}}/uploads/<filename>`

## Comments & ratings

`Comment` links a **product** and a **user**, and refers to itself through `parentComment` for one-level-deep replies. Every create / update / delete recalculates the product's `averageRating` and `numReviews`, so product listings can sort and filter on rating without touching the comments collection.

See the **Comments** folder for the full contract.

## Realtime events (Socket.IO)

The API also runs a Socket.IO server on the **same port**. Clients connect with credentials (`withCredentials: true`) and the server reads the same auth cookie from the handshake, then puts the socket into rooms:

| Room | Who | Events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `everyone` | every client, guests included | `product:new` |
| `user:<id>` | one customer | `order:status`, `order:payment` |
| `admins` | all logged-in admins | `order:new`, `order:payment` |

Emitted from `product.controller` (create), `order.controller` (create, status change) and `payment.controller` (webhook). A status change only fires when the status actually changed — editing an address does not notify the customer.

## Quick start

1. Select the **bano-qabil-local** environment (top-right of Postman).
2. Start the server: `npm run dev` inside `backend/`.
3. Run **Auth → Register (Admin)**, then **Auth → Login** — the token is captured automatically.
4. Everything else is ready to send.

## Error contract

Every error response — including 404s for unknown routes — is produced by one central handler and always has this shape:

```json
{ "message": "..." }
```

| Cause | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Malformed ObjectId (`CastError`) | `400` — `Invalid _id: <value>` |
| Schema validation failure | `400` — all failing fields, comma-separated |
| Duplicate unique field | `400` — `<field> already exists` |
| Malformed JSON body | `400` — `Invalid JSON body` |
| Missing/invalid/expired JWT | `401` |
| Role or ownership check | `403` |
| Unknown route | `404` — `Route not found - <METHOD> <path>` |
| Unhandled bug | `500` — generic message in production |
